how-much-to-charge-to-install-a-mini-spl.text:
← Mini-split install bid calculator

How much to charge to install a mini split

Price the job from cost, then convert to dollars per head. Do not start from a published per-head or per-ton number and work backwards. Two single-zone 12k installs can differ by a couple of thousand dollars once the line-set, the height, and the electrical service are in the bid.

Open the free bid calculator

What a per-head quote cannot see

Outdoor units and indoor heads mostly scale with count. These do not:

  • Line-set beyond the 15–25 ft the equipment quote already includes
  • A ceiling cassette or concealed ducted head versus a high-wall mount
  • A second- or third-story install, or a tall first-floor wall that needs a ladder
  • A new 240 V circuit, a relocated disconnect, or a subpanel
  • A condensate pump when there is no gravity path
  • Permit fees and travel that are a trip and a check, not a head

If you match a cheaper per-head quote that was written for a first-floor wall-mount and an existing disconnect, you are matching someone else's job, not yours.

A bid that holds together

  1. Size the system from head count × BTU, not a rounded marketing ton.
  2. Time indoor labor as hours per head on an easy wall, then multiply by head type and story.
  3. Add extra line-set as its own feet, material, and hours. Those hours climb with height.
  4. Add electrical and condensate extras as their own hours and material. They do not shrink when the job is a single zone.
  5. Load the wage (taxes, workers' compensation, insurance, PTO). Price from loaded labor, not take-home.
  6. Add permits and travel.
  7. Recover overhead as a percent of direct cost, then set margin as a share of the customer's price.
  8. Only then look at price per head — and at the walk-away price if a homeowner asks you to sharpen it.

What this is not

This is not a Manual J load calculation, a permit approval, a refrigerant-handling certification, a code inspection, or tax or rebate advice. It is arithmetic on numbers you enter. Confirm equipment, line-set path, electrical and condensate scope, and every invoice before you send a price.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a mini split?

Charge from your own cost: outdoor unit, indoor heads, branch box, crew hours times a head-type and story factor, extra line-set feet, electrical extras, condensate, permits, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. Convert that price to dollars per head at the end for comparison, not as the bid method.

Why is a per-head quote dangerous?

Equipment scales with heads. Extra line-set, a ceiling cassette, a second story, a condensate pump, and a new 240 V circuit do not. Those extras can erase the margin on a quote that looked fine on a first-floor wall-mount of the same capacity.

Does this include a load calculation or rebate?

No. The calculator prices the install. Manual J, permits, refrigerant handling, and utility rebates are the installer's, the AHJ's, or the program administrator's to apply. Do not treat the tool as a load, code, or net-cost determination.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or electrical-code advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

index.html.text:
FOR MINI-SPLIT INSTALLERS

Bid the run and the circuit, not the head.

A flat per-head quote treats a first-floor 12k wall-mount with 15 ft of line-set as the same job as a second-story cassette with a 50 ft run, a condensate pump, and a new 240 V circuit. Price the heads, the line-set extras, the height, and the electrical extras separately — then see the price, the dollars per head, and the number below which the job loses money.

The system

Start from a common residential layout, then replace head count and BTU with the equipment you actually quoted.

The run and the service

Head type and story multiply indoor labor. Extra line-set hours also climb with height. Electrical extras are a fixed adder — they do not get cheaper on a single-zone job.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. Matching a cheaper per-head quote after leaving it out is how a sold job becomes a loss.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the cost goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Head-type factors, story factors, and extras are common ballpark starting points, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why is equipment nearly two-thirds of the cost?

    Because a mini-split is an equipment job with an install attached. On the defaults — one 12,000 BTU head — the outdoor unit is $1,400 and the indoor head $550, which is 64.1% of direct cost against 14.4% for the eight hours of labor. Your margin is far more sensitive to what you pay for equipment than to how fast the crew works, which is the opposite of most trades on this site.

    Why is the line set $0 when the job clearly needs one?

    Because the first 15 feet per head is in the base equipment price, and the default run is exactly 15 feet. Only footage past the allowance bills, and it bills in labor as well as material — roughly an hour per extra ten feet, since a longer run means more penetration, hanging, and evacuation time. A second-floor head on a long run is where this number moves.

    Is $325 per thousand BTU a rate I can quote from?

    Not across sizes. It is $3,902.33 divided by 12 kBTU, and it drops as capacity rises because the permit, travel, commissioning hour, and trip are the same for a bigger head. A 24,000 BTU single-head system does not cost twice as much. The figure is for checking one quote against another at the same capacity, not for scaling.

    Why doesn’t a 22% target margin mean adding 22% to cost?

    Because margin is a fraction of the price. The default system costs $3,043.82, and holding 22% of the price as profit is $3,043.82 ÷ 0.78 = $3,902.33. Adding 22% to cost gives $3,713.46, an 18% margin — and on an equipment-heavy job like this one, where the cost base is large, that gap is $189 on a single head and scales with every head you add.

vs-a-flat-2800-per-head-quote.html.text:
← Mini-Split Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $2,800-a-head quote

“$2,800 a head” is not a price for a mini-split install — it is a price for one specific floor, head type, and line-set length, quietly applied to every head that calls in.

What a flat price per head is

A flat rate per head is the fastest way to quote a ductless install: multiply the head count by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a search-result special or a competitor's flyer will call and ask you to match, whatever their job actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a first-floor wall-mount with a short line-set already covered by the equipment quote, an existing 240 V disconnect, and a gravity drain — and then reused for every install afterward, whether or not the next head looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter head count and BTU size, head type, story height, total line-set feet against what the equipment quote already includes, and electrical and condensate extras, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the story, the line-set, and every extra separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this head, not a generic one.

What a flat price per head doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/head on a first-floor slab and a third-story ceiling cassette, even though indoor and line-set labor climb with every floor. Prices story height as a separate factor on indoor and line-set labor, so a second- or third-story head costs more than the same head at grade.
Has no line for line-set feet beyond what the equipment quote already includes, regardless of whether the run is 15 ft or 50 ft. Prices only the extra feet beyond the included length, by hours and material, so a long run costs more than a short one.
Charges the same rate for a standard wall mount as for a ceiling cassette or concealed ducted head, or for existing electrical as for a new 240 V circuit and a condensate pump. Prices head type, electrical extras, and condensate separately, so a cassette with new electrical and a pump costs more than a wall mount on existing service.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-head rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two heads, the same floor-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($42/hr installer wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, a 22% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $3,902.33/head rateGap
Single-zone 12k wall-mount, first floor, 15 ft line-set fully included, existing electrical, gravity drain — the job the rate is set from$3,902.33 bid price; $3,043.82 break-even cost$3,902.33 (exactly $3,902.33/head — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
Single-zone 18k wall-mount, second story, 35 ft line-set (20 ft beyond included), new 20-30A circuit, condensate pump$6,140.00 bid price; $4,789.20 break-even cost$3,902.33The rate quotes $886.86 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $2,237.66 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $3,902.33/head rate is not invented, and it is not the marketing $2,800 figure either — it is this calculator's own price on the first-floor wall-mount preset, divided by that preset's own head count. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the second-story head, it never sees the extra line-set, the new circuit, or the condensate pump at all. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-head rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one head it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per head get a mini-split install bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is story height, line-set feet beyond what the equipment quote already includes, head type, and electrical and condensate extras -- not a blended head count. Equipment cost scales with heads reasonably well, but a second-story head with extra line-set, a new 240 V circuit, and a condensate pump is doing far more labor than the same single head on a first-floor slab with a short included line-set and an existing disconnect, none of which shows up in the head count a flat rate is built from.

What does a flat price per head usually leave out entirely?

Line-set feet beyond the length the equipment quote already includes, story height (indoor and line-set labor climb with each floor), head type (a ceiling cassette or concealed ducted head costs more labor than a standard wall mount), a new or upgraded 240 V circuit, and a condensate pump where gravity drainage is not available. A first-floor wall-mount with a short included line-set is doing far less than a second-story head needing extra line-set, new electrical, and a pump -- and a per-head number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: a single-zone 12k wall-mount on the first floor with 15 ft of included line-set prices at $3,902.33, or $3,902.33 a head. Applying that same rate to a single-zone 18k wall-mount on the second story with 35 ft of line-set (20 ft beyond the included length), a new 20-30A circuit, and a condensate pump quotes $3,902.33 for a job that actually breaks even at $4,789.20 -- $886.86 short before a dollar of profit, and $2,237.66 below the calculator's own $6,140.00 bid price.

Is a flat price per head ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- first floor, standard wall mount, line-set within the included length, existing electrical, gravity drain -- a per-head rate can land close, and on this calculator's own easy preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which head it was built on and neither does the estimator until story, line-set, head type, and electrical and condensate extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes head count and BTU size, head type, story height, line-set feet, and electrical and condensate extras, plus the labor hours, equipment costs, and wage you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-head rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running an HVAC company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one mini-split install cost, given its heads, height, and extras, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, electrical, plumbing, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the HVAC trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's head count and BTU size, head type (wall, floor, cassette, ducted, or mixed) and story height, extra line-set feet past the included allowance, electrical extras (an existing disconnect through a new subpanel), and a condensate pump where gravity drainage is not available, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, permit, travel and lift, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per head, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and an HVAC shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
